title: Event-Grounded Sparse Autoencoders for Vision-Language-Action Policies
models: LoRA-finetuned pi0.5 on Mobile ALOHA (real robot)
action_head: discrete action tokens (OpenVLA) and flow/diffusion action expert (pi0.5)
methods: per-token BatchTopK SAEs (k=64) on post-block residual stream
Hooked SR (closed-loop success with SAE reconstruction inserted) as fidelity metric
kinematic keyframes via Automatic Waypoint Extraction + task-local event clustering (visual, state, progress), optional VLM labels
four feature rankings (event-aligned, window-mean, task-mean, random-alive)
residual-preserving latent edits (zero-out and soft scaling)
question: Can SAE features be ranked against behavior-derived events instead of text contexts, and do the top-ranked features causally matter for closed-loop VLA success?
key_findings: Offline reconstruction does not predict closed-loop fidelity: OpenVLA SAEs have FVE 0.91-0.999, but Hooked SR is 0% at layers 16 and 24 (0.2% at layer 0) and 34.8% at layer 31 vs ~64-70% raw; pi0.5 keeps >=95% Hooked SR at every probed backbone and expert layer (Table 1).
OpenVLA SAE alive fraction falls from 94.1% at layer 0 to 3.1-8.0% at deeper layers.

OpenVLA layer 31 single-feature zero-out (top 5 per ranking): event-aligned drops SR 70.0% -> 48.8% (-21.2) vs window-mean -6.2, task-mean -6.5, random-alive -1.3 (Table 3); the top three features carry nearly all of the drop.
pi0.5 PaliGemma backbone: single-feature zero-out changes SR by at most ~3 points at any layer and ranking; even dropping 16 features jointly gives only moderate change.

pi0.5 action expert: zeroing almost any single feature, including random alive ones, collapses SR to ~0% at layers 0, 5, 11 (layer 17 less: event-aligned -0.7, window-mean -23.4) (Table 3), i.e. broad sensitivity rather than event selectivity.
Features chosen for one task disrupt other tasks about equally (target/off-target probe).

Soft scaling gives a monotonic but steep SR transition. On the real robot, mild suppression of action-expert features at layer 17 increases distance to the prompted chip colour; aggressive edits destabilize the arm.

evidence.scale: 50 closed-loop rollouts per task for discovery; Hooked SR with 10 rollouts per task; K=5 (OpenVLA) or K=3 (pi0.5) features per ranking; real-robot trial counts not stated in main text
evidence.statistics: partial: mean +/- SD across suites for fidelity; Delta SR point estimates for interventions; no significance tests
evidence.baselines: random-alive feature control, window-mean and task-mean rankings, FFN value-vector baseline (Haon et al.) on hardware in appendix

causal_validation: Yes: single-feature zero-out and soft scaling in closed loop, compared against a random-alive feature control; plus hardware dose-response.
closed_loop: Yes: LIBERO closed-loop rollouts and a real Mobile ALOHA task.
limitations_stated: Selected features are shared across tasks, not task-specific; on the action expert even random features collapse behavior, so single-feature edits do not isolate one behavioral factor.
VLM-derived event semantics are only used for visualization, not ranking.
Binary success is coarse; strong edits destabilize the real robot, so only mild interventions were tested.
critique: The pi0.5 SAEs are 1x width (2048->2048 and 1024->1024) with k=64, so they are not overcomplete dictionaries. Zeroing one latent removes a substantial share of the representation, which likely explains why even random action-expert features collapse the policy. The 'broad sensitivity' is partly an artifact of the dictionary size.

OpenVLA results are confined to layer 31 because SAE insertion breaks earlier layers (consistent with 2603.19233). The positive event-aligned result therefore concerns a layer next to the action head and 5 features.
The random-alive control is a good design choice and is what makes the OpenVLA result credible; it also exposes that the action-expert rankings carry no specific information.
Real-robot evidence is a dose-response figure with unstated trial counts; it shows feature edits can perturb prompt-following, not that features are interpretable.
Honest negative framing ('sparse but imperfect causal basis') is useful counter-evidence to more optimistic SAE claims in 2603.19183.
one_line: Ranking SAE features by how their activations line up with kinematic events finds OpenVLA features whose removal clearly hurts success, but in pi0.5 the backbone barely reacts to single-feature edits while the action expert collapses under almost any edit, so SAE features are only a coarse causal handle.
